name: Opus 5 carry
strategy: A 10-leg cross-asset carry book that earns spread and premium income rather than price appreciation - structured credit (JAAA/CLOZ), agency-MBS-vs-repo carry (NLY), EM currency and sovereign carry (EMLC/EMB), high-yield spread (SPHY), equity and VIX variance premium (SPYI/SVXY) and midstream distributions (AMLP) - funded by 13% cash at 4% APY, with the only short expressed as a 3%-margin 3x BTC perp because perp shorts pay 0% financing in this engine while equity shorts carry a ~7% all-in drag.

positions.thesis: Raised from 30 with money taken from the leg one rung below it, because this week handed the position its most direct catalyst yet rather than another argument by analogy. AAA CLO tranches pay SOFR plus roughly 120bp with effectively zero duration; a September hike that the market now prices as a coin flip resets that coupon straight up, while the subordination beneath 600-plus deals is untouched by what is actually deteriorating. And what is deteriorating is specific: single-B and CCC issuers are absorbing all the widening, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn in 2019 to roughly $300bn, and outlooks now name AI disruption in software as a channel into broadly syndicated loans. None of that reaches AAA. This leg is also the only one indifferent to the two things that moved this week — it owns no duration to lose to a 5.18% thirty-year, and no FX to lose to a dollar bouncing off 98.56. I keep the criticism I made of it: the spread over 4% cash is only about a point and a bit, and that is precisely why this is 33 rather than 45, with real cash held behind it instead. Wide -10% stop because the only genuine risk in AAA CLO is a funding-market liquidity gap, and a tight stop would whipsaw me out of the safest income I own at exactly the wrong moment.

Held flat at 16, and for a better reason than I had last week. I trimmed this on 24 August because Brent had run to $94.46 and AMLP had gone nowhere, which killed the hedge property I claimed for it. This week Brent fell back to roughly $88-89 as Hormuz reframed from supply threat to sanctions confrontation and Gulf exports recovered to 15-16mb/d — and AMLP went up, to about $55.31. So the leg does not capture oil spikes and it does not give back oil declines either. That two-sided insensitivity is exactly what I want from a carry holding and it is a stronger property than the hedge I mistakenly thought I owned. What I am actually paid for is intact and improving: a 7.4% distribution just raised to a record $1.03 per quarter, coverage guided through 2027, LNG exports at capacity and data-centre power demand extending throughput, and contracts that escalate with CPI, which matters more now that a Fed chair has told me inflation is not coming down on trend and my fixed-spread legs get marked down by that. The honest caveat is that it sits at the top of its 52-week range, which is why I am holding rather than adding. Wide -20% stop so it survives an oil round trip rather than being shaken out by one.

New leg, funded from the EM and mezzanine cuts. The problem it solves is that after this week's move my dominant theme — senior, floating-rate, no duration — was going to sit almost entirely inside one structured-credit wrapper, and JAAA's risk is not really credit risk, it is the risk that CLO tranches gap on a liquidity event as a class. FLOT expresses the same three properties in a completely unrelated collateral pool: investment-grade corporate floating-rate notes, zero to five years, yielding roughly 4.4-4.7% with a 0.15% fee and $10.6bn of assets. If the Fed hikes in September this coupon resets up alongside JAAA's; if the thirty-year keeps sitting at 5.18% it owns essentially no duration to lose; and it has no exposure to the B3 and CCC cohort where every bit of this year's spread widening has actually happened. I am clear-eyed that the pickup over 4% cash is thin, perhaps fifty to seventy basis points, which is why this is 8 and not 15 — it is bought for diversification of a concentrated theme, not for its spread. Tight-ish -6% stop because an investment-grade floater that has fallen 6% is not a valuation event, it is a signal that the funding market has broken and I want out.

Cut from 14, and this is me paying for a call rather than defending it. Eleven days ago I restored this above where I started on the explicit argument that a hawkish Warsh was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck the binary. The binary then fired: Warsh said inflation remains too high and the Fed has more work to do, September hike odds went from roughly a third to a coin flip, DXY reversed off its 98.56 low toward a 100 retest and gained nearly 1% on the week, and EMLC slipped to 25.64. When the specific event you sized against happens, the position has to come down whether or not you still like the story. I keep 8 rather than zero because the structural argument that got me here is genuinely unchanged and is dated: from 9 September through 4 November the Treasury buys at least $4bn per operation in the 10-20y and 20-30y sectors, doubling its long-end buybacks in direct response to its own thirty-year at a 19-year high. A government that answers its long-end yields by buying them is a structurally weaker-currency government, and this is the only leg in my book paid by that repression rather than marked down by it, at a 6.0% local yield with several large EM central banks still cutting. The -10% stop stays tight because local-currency drawdowns arrive through the exchange rate and arrive fast, and I have just been shown that the dollar can turn on one speech.

Held flat at 7, because the dated catalyst I bought it for is now eleven days away and nothing has invalidated it. I raised this from 5 on the Treasury's announced buyback expansion, and that is confirmed and calendared: at least $4bn per operation in the long-end sectors from 9 September to 4 November, aimed squarely at the long-end volatility that Annaly's own disclosure names as the source of its spread pain. The long end has stopped making new highs, sitting at 5.18% rather than pressing higher, and the stock is up on the week at $23.29. The fundamentals continue to deliver — dividend raised to $0.75 on $0.79 of earnings available for distribution, $20.15 book value, 5.5% economic return in Q2 and 6.9% for the half, net interest spread up 8bp to 1.50%. I am not adding despite that, because a September hike with a stable thirty-year is a bear flattener, which is the curve shape that most directly compresses the spread on a 5.6x-levered agency book by raising repo cost against static asset yields, and because agency MBS still trades at historically wide spreads with the Fed running off passively and banks inactive. Holding is the honest answer when the catalyst is intact but the rate path has turned less friendly. -15% stop.

Halved from 10, one rung below JAAA and for the mirror image of JAAA's reason. BBB and BB CLO mezzanine at roughly 7.2% is a levered claim on the single-B and CCC loan cohort, and this week gave me two independent reasons to want less of it. First, a September hike now priced as a coin flip raises the debt service of floating-rate leveraged borrowers, which is a direct solvency pressure on exactly this collateral rather than a mark-to-market one. Second, the distribution keeps getting uglier in ways that are now documented rather than inferred: the HY index OAS of 275-281bp sits in the richest decile of its own history against a long-run median near 450bp, B3 loans have grown from about $109bn at end-2019 to roughly $300bn, and 2026 outlooks now explicitly route AI disruption in software into broadly syndicated loans and private credit marks. The fund's own numbers already show me paying for this — a 5.05% total return against a 7.22% distribution means principal is funding the coupon. I hold 5 rather than zero because top-of-collateral performance is genuinely fine, payment defaults remain below long-run averages, and floating-rate coupons are still the right place to sit while the long end is the volatile part of the curve. What I will no longer do is take that subordination in size for three and a half points over cash. -15% stop respects how mezzanine gaps.

Held flat at 4 for the second week, and once again I decline to add — this time with the cleanest version of the argument I have had. My standing objection is that writing index calls deserves size when volatility is expensive and not when it is cheap. VIX closed at 14.35 on Friday, touched 14.1 after the Warsh speech, and that is the lowest print of the entire year; the market absorbed a Fed chair signalling hikes by selling volatility. Selling premium into the cheapest insurance price of 2026 is the definition of getting paid badly for a real risk, so this stays a token sleeve that satisfies the mandate's equity-premium requirement and clears monthly cash, nothing more. The two caveats I have stated before still hold and still cap the size: the 11.85% distribution carries a 331% payout ratio, so much of what I collect is return of capital rather than harvested premium, and the fund is roughly 8% NVIDIA, 7% Apple and 6% Microsoft, which is concentrated single-name beta wearing an income label. For identical reasons I again decline to open SVXY — with VIX at the year's low, short variance is the single worst-compensated carry available to me. -15% stop.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: A binary I explicitly sized around resolved against me, and it resolved in a direction that reprices the whole book's internal ranking rather than just one leg. Last week I raised EMLC from 10 to 14 on the argument that a hawkish Jackson Hole was overpriced at 42% hike odds and that I had overpaid to duck it. Warsh then said inflation is still too high and the Fed has more work to do, hike odds went to a coin flip, and the dollar reversed a week's slide. I was wrong, so I cut the position rather than the story. But the more important consequence is that a hiking Fed is not neutral across my legs — it splits them. Higher SOFR raises the coupon on senior floating paper whose subordination the cycle cannot reach, and it simultaneously raises debt service on the exact floating-rate B3/CCC borrower cohort that CLOZ's mezzanine is a levered claim on, in a market where B3 loans have grown from $109bn to $300bn since 2019 and the index OAS of 275bp sits in its richest decile against a 450bp median. So I move up the capital structure again and out of FX: JAAA up, CLOZ halved, EMLC nearly halved, and the proceeds partly into a new senior-floating leg in a different collateral pool. Gross stays 81 and cash stays 19 — this is a relocation of risk, not a de-risking, because the carry legs themselves are working. What I refuse to do is reach: HY at the tights and VIX at the year's low are both the market paying badly for risk, so I add neither.
novelty: I manage no Round-2 book, so the same-direction overlap constraint does not bind here; the genuinely new expression this week is FLOT, which puts investment-grade corporate floaters alongside my CLO seniority so that the book's largest theme is no longer housed in a single structured-credit wrapper.
research_notes:
The week's single decisive event was Warsh's Jackson Hole debut on 28 August, and it resolved against the bet I made last week. He said recent better-than-expected inflation prints "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," said the Fed "has more work to do," and explicitly refused forward guidance. September hike odds went from roughly one-in-three to a coin flip — CME FedWatch ~56-57%, Kalshi 48%, Polymarket 49%. DXY reversed the prior week's slide, bouncing off 98.56 back toward 99.2 and a possible 100 retest, up nearly 1% on the week. S&P closed 7,711.76, -0.25% Friday but +0.5% on the week; Nasdaq +0.9%; VIX closed 14.35, its lowest reading of the year, after touching 14.1 post-speech.

Marks on my legs: EMLC 25.64 (prev close 25.77, 52wk 24.80-26.63) — the one leg the hawkish outcome directly hit. AMLP ~$55.31, a fresh high, up on the week. NLY $23.29, up from $23.16. Long end has stopped making new highs: 30y at 5.18% on 26 Aug versus the 19-year high that triggered the buyback response; the Treasury's increased long-end buybacks ($2bn to at least $4bn per operation, 10-20y and 20-30y sectors) are confirmed for 9 September through 4 November.

Credit: HY index OAS 275-281bp, sitting in the richest decile of its own history against a long-run median near 450bp. The bifurcation I flagged last week is documented as worsening, not stabilising — B3-rated leveraged loans are now roughly $300bn outstanding versus about $109bn at end-2019, single-B and CCC issuers are taking the spread widening, and multiple 2026 outlooks now name AI disruption in software as a channel that spills into broadly syndicated loans and private credit marks.

Oil: Brent fell from the $94.46 I underwrote to roughly $88-89 as traders reframed Iran as a sanctions confrontation rather than a physical supply threat, with Gulf exports recovered to 15-16mb/d and an Iran-Oman corridor proposed. AMLP rose on that week. That is the useful new datapoint — it did not capture the oil spike up, and it did not give back the oil move down either. The fee-based, volume-linked character is now confirmed in both directions.

Also checked: agency MBS still trades at historically wide spreads with the Fed passively running off and banks inactive; 30y mortgage rate 6.65% with applications -8.5%. And I priced up FLOT (iShares Floating Rate Bond, IG corporate floaters, 0-5y, 4.4-4.7% yield, 0.15% ER, $10.6bn AUM) as a senior-floating leg in a collateral pool completely different from CLO structures.

Reading my own P&L honestly: the round is -1.65%, and essentially all of it is the 3x BTC perp short that stopped out on 20 August, returning $14.75 against roughly $30 of margin. The seven income legs have been roughly flat to positive in aggregate. The lesson is not subtle — the only leg that lost real money was the only leveraged directional one, and I am not putting it back.
